query: For initially solid iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles examined across the premelting and melting regime, limited understanding of their thermal response constrains interpretation of application limits and high-temperature synthesis, where cooling must consolidate the solid solution. Prior studies of Ag, Au, Al, and Pd nanoparticles established that nanoscale phase-transition behavior can differ markedly among particle systems, but findings from single-metal particles do not resolve the response of chemically complex nanoparticles. Work on bimetallic particles further demonstrated that chemical complexity can produce varied configurations, while research on high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles remains sparse and has not established the governing physics for this composition. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its premelting and melting behavior and why? Define a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline particle, the limits within which the hypothesis should apply, prior findings that support it, and an observation that would decisively falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Due to their high configurational entropy, iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper HEA nanoparticles develop intrinsic local lattice distortions that produce a range of local melting temperatures. Under controlled heating in an inert atmosphere, the limited atomic mobility minimizes rapid elemental segregation, resulting in a broadened and gradual premelting behavior compared to simpler single‐metal or bimetallic nanoparticles.
generation.material_initial_state: Initially solid, uniformly distributed, single-phase iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
generation.intervention: Controlled heating (thermal ramping) under an inert atmosphere.
generation.conditions: Nanoscale particles (<20 nm) subjected to a uniform and controlled heating rate in an inert or vacuum environment; comparisons are made with single-metal or bimetallic nanoparticles of similar size.
generation.structural_mediator: High configurational entropy–induced local lattice distortions, coupled with limited atomic diffusion.
generation.mechanism: Upon heating, the intrinsic lattice distortions create a distribution of local melting temperatures, while sluggish atomic mobility suppresses rapid elemental segregation. This interplay causes the onset of melting to be gradual and spatially heterogeneous, rather than a sharp, simultaneous transition.
generation.predicted_outcome: The HEA nanoparticles will show a broadened premelting regime—for example, exhibiting gradual loss of crystalline order and broad DSC peaks—while maintaining a relatively homogeneous elemental distribution, in contrast to baseline nanoparticles which melt sharply.
generation.baseline: Single-metal or bimetallic nanoparticles of comparable size, which demonstrate sharp melting transitions and pronounced, uniform melting behavior.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to nanoscale HEA particles (<20 nm) heated under controlled conditions in inert environments, where extrinsic factors such as oxidation or particle coalescence are minimized.
generation.uncertainty: The exact impact of particle size and heating rate on the extent of premelting broadening remains to be fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize HEA nanoparticles alongside similarly sized single-metal or bimetallic nanoparticles. Heat both samples in an inert atmosphere using a controlled thermal ramp, and monitor the melting behavior in situ.
measurements: Differential scanning calorimetry to track the onset and breadth of melting transitions
In situ TEM and X-ray diffraction to observe structural evolution and phase changes
Elemental mapping (EDS or atom probe tomography) to detect any occurrence of elemental segregation during heating
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA nanoparticles exhibit a melting behavior that is as sharp as that of the baseline samples or if significant early elemental segregation is observed during heating, the hypothesis would be considered falsified.

Naturally, this model offers an idealized perspective and does not reflect all experimental details. In reality, there will be distinct mixing enthalpies between the elements. This will introduce a preference for certain structures which is opposed by the limited mobility of atoms. This explains how a rather mixed particle is obtained in the synthesis for a five-element mixture, which is restricted in the binary case, but also sees signs of local segregation in the NMF analysis. The model relates well to the single-source precursor synthesis, where a solid precursor is reduced at moderate temperatures, hence limiting the free mobility. Extending this approach to other syntheses with similar solid, mixed precursors can thus provide a viable way to design new low-temperature approaches for small high entropy alloy nanoparticles. Simultaneous in situ X-ray diffraction and multi-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy experiments allowed us to study the formation mechanism of noble metal bimetallic and high entropy alloy nanoparticles in depth. The samples were prepared by reduction of single-source precursors. For five-element mixtures, the formation of a single phase occurs more readily than in the binary samples. Under the studied reaction conditions, single-phase formation for binary alloys was restricted to systems where cooperative reduction occurred, while single-phase HEA particles could be obtained even though the elements were reduced consecutively. The findings are explained with a stochastic model that simulates the particle formation process. Regardless of the element interactions, the model quantifies that it is more likely to form a random alloy if more atom types are present in a system with limited free atom mobility. This highlights that knowledge of the formation mechanism is crucial for understanding the material formation pathways. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) contain five or more principal elements in equimolar or near-equimolar ratios. When the size of HEAs decreases to nanoscale, such as nanoparticles, the high specific surface area, quantum size effect, strong synergistic interaction, and lattice distortion make them an ideal platform for a variety of surface reactions, showing great promise for a wide range of emerging energy-related applications, particularly in the field of catalysis. There are two categories of methods for the preparation of high-entropy alloy nanoparticles (HEA NPs), generally classified as the “top-down” physical methods by crushing bulk materials and the “bottom-up” chemical methods by reducing metal salt precursors. The HEA NPs prepared by ball milling usually display a large distribution in the composition. Wet chemical synthesis can effectively control the composition, phase structure, and particle size of the target elements. drafts.hypothesis: The premelting and melting of initially solid iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles is governed by differential elemental mobility that causes low–melting-point elements (e.g., copper) to segregate to the nanoparticle surfaces. This surface segregation creates local compositional gradients which destabilize the solid solution at the surface, leading to an onset of premelting at lower temperatures than in uniform, single-component nanoparticles.
drafts.material_initial_state: Uniformly distributed, solid iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
drafts.intervention: Controlled heating (thermal ramp) under an inert atmosphere to progressively approach and exceed premelting temperatures.
drafts.conditions: Nanoparticles with high surface‐to‐volume ratios (e.g., 5–100 nm) are heated at controlled rates in an inert or vacuum environment. A direct comparison is made with single‐metal or less chemically complex bimetallic nanoparticles manufactured to similar size distributions.
drafts.structural_mediator: Surface regions exhibiting compositional gradients due to elemental segregation (particularly enrichment of lower melting point copper) act as the mediator by locally reducing the structural stability.
drafts.mechanism: As temperature increases, differences in atomic mobility lead to preferential migration of copper atoms (and possibly other lower melting point constituents) to the surface. This segregation disrupts the uniformity of the solid solution and reduces the local cohesive energy, thereby lowering the melting onset temperature at the surfaces compared to the interior. The premelting thus initiates heterogeneously, with the surface showing early disordering before the core melts.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Measurements will reveal that HEA nanoparticles exhibit an earlier onset of surface premelting (i.e., at lower temperatures) and a spatially heterogeneous melting behavior relative to baseline single-metal or binary nanoparticles. Atom-probe or similar compositional analyses should detect an enrichment of the lower melting point element(s) at the particle surfaces during heating.
drafts.baseline: Single-component metal nanoparticles (or binary nanoparticles with reduced chemical complexity) of comparable size, which are expected to have a more uniform melting behavior without pronounced premature surface melting.
drafts.boundary: This hypothesis applies to nanoscale particles (approximately 5–100 nm) heated under conditions that avoid extrinsic effects such as oxidation or coalescence. Its validity is confined to systems where kinetic factors allow for measurable elemental segregation during the heating timescale.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize high-entropy alloy nanoparticles and baseline single-metal (or bimetallic) nanoparticles of similar sizes. Heat samples using a controlled thermal ramp in an inert environment. Simultaneously monitor structural changes via high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) and assess elemental distributions using atom-probe tomography or energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) during heating.
measurements: Temperature at which surface premelting initiates
Spatial distribution of elements (especially copper) across the nanoparticles during heating
Progression and propagation rate of the melting front within individual particles
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA nanoparticles do not show a significantly lower surface premelting onset temperature compared to baseline particles, or if compositional analysis shows no preferential enrichment of copper (or other low-melting elements) at the surface during heating, then the hypothesis would be considered falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper high-entropy alloy nanoparticles, local lattice distortions and compositional heterogeneity arising from high configurational entropy expand the temperature range over which premelting occurs, thereby shifting the melting onset relative to single‐metal nanoparticles.
drafts.intervention: Controlled heating of the nanoparticles using a defined and uniform heating protocol.
drafts.conditions: Experiments conducted in an inert atmosphere with a uniform heating rate across the temperature range near the expected melting regime.
drafts.structural_mediator: Local lattice strain and nanoscale compositional fluctuations within the nanoparticles.
drafts.mechanism: The inherent high configurational entropy in the alloy induces significant lattice distortions and local chemical inhomogeneity. These factors create a distribution of local melting temperatures within each nanoparticle, leading to a broadened and staggered onset of atomic mobility (premelting) prior to complete melting.
drafts.predicted_outcome: High-entropy nanoparticles will display an extended premelting regime (evidenced by broadened DSC peaks and gradual loss of crystalline order), contrasting with the sharper melting transitions observed in similar single-metal nanoparticles.
drafts.baseline: Single-metal nanoparticles of comparable size, which typically exhibit narrow, well-defined melting transitions with minimal premelting behavior.
drafts.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for nanoparticles of similar nanoscale dimensions under inert, controlled heating conditions. Deviations in particle size, composition, or environmental conditions may produce different thermal responses.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of nanoparticles: one set of Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy alloy nanoparticles and a control set of single-metal nanoparticles of similar size. Heat both sets under identical conditions while monitoring thermal transitions and structural evolution.
measurements: Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to track onset, peak, and completion temperatures of melting.
In-situ transmission electron microscopy (TEM) or X-ray diffraction (XRD) to observe the development of lattice disorder and phase changes.
Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) to check for local compositional variations during heating.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-entropy alloy nanoparticles do not exhibit a broader or staggered premelting regime relative to the single-metal nanoparticles (i.e., if their DSC curves and structural evolution profiles show a sharp, single-stage melting similar to the control), then the proposed hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: The premelting and melting behavior of iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles is governed by a kinetic suppression of atomic diffusion that, in combination with high configurational entropy, traps a stochastic single-phase solid solution. This mechanism delays surface premelting and limits local elemental segregation compared to simpler (e.g., bimetallic) systems.
drafts.material_initial_state: Solid, single-phase high-entropy alloy nanoparticles (composed of Fe, Ni, Cr, Co, Cu) with a homogeneous atomic distribution in a solid-solution lattice.
drafts.intervention: Controlled ramp heating from ambient temperature through the premelting region into full melting conditions under an inert atmosphere.
drafts.conditions: Nanoparticles with diameters in the 3–10 nm range, heated at a controlled rate (e.g., few °C/s) in an inert environment, where atomic mobility is limited by the solid-state and kinetic barriers.
drafts.structural_mediator: The intrinsic lattice distortion and high configurational entropy of the multi-element system, combined with limited atomic diffusivity at the nanoscale, mediate the retention of a uniform solid-solution structure even as melting begins.
drafts.mechanism: Because the diverse atomic species are more dilute and their mutual diffusion is kinetically hindered in the nanoparticle’s solid state, local atomic rearrangements that would normally lead to segregation during premelting are suppressed. This stochastic mixing effect helps delay the onset of surface melting and prevents the formation of compositionally segregated liquid domains prior to complete melting.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Under controlled heating, HEA nanoparticles will exhibit a more uniform, delayed surface premelting and minimal elemental segregation compared to baseline bimetallic or elemental nanoparticles. Their melting onset will occur over a narrower temperature range, preserving the single-phase nature for longer in the premelting regime.
drafts.baseline: Comparable nanoparticles of bimetallic or single-metal systems (of similar size and morphology) which are known to exhibit earlier localized surface melting and more pronounced compositional segregation under the same heating conditions.
drafts.boundary: This hypothesis applies to nanoparticles in the nanometer size range (approximately 3–10 nm) and within a temperature window approaching, but not greatly exceeding, the full melting point, where limited atomic mobility is a dominant factor.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform in situ high-resolution TEM and X-ray diffraction during controlled ramp heating of the HEA nanoparticles alongside control samples (bimetallic or single-metal nanoparticles) under identical conditions. Use elemental mapping (EDS) to monitor any onset of segregation or formation of distinct surface melt phases.
measurements: In situ TEM images with real-time elemental mapping (EDS) to track atomic distribution changes during heating
XRD profiles to monitor phase changes and emergence of secondary phases
Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to detect exothermic or endothermic events associated with phase segregation or premelting transitions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA nanoparticles display evidence of early localized surface melting or clear compositional segregation (comparable to or more pronounced than that observed in the baseline bimetallic or elemental nanoparticles) before reaching the full melting temperature, this would decisively falsify the hypothesis that kinetic suppression of atomic diffusion and high configurational entropy govern a delayed, uniform premelting behavior.

drafts.hypothesis: The premelting and melting behavior of iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper HEA nanoparticles is governed by a stochastic, homogeneous nucleation process that is enforced by high configurational entropy and limited atomic mobility. This mechanism prevents local phase segregation and yields a broadened, gradual transition from solid to liquid, unlike the sharper, more phase‐segregated behavior observed in bimetallic or monometallic nanoparticles.
drafts.material_initial_state: Initially solid, single-phase iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles with a random distribution of constituent atoms and built-in lattice strain.
drafts.intervention: Apply controlled heating (and subsequent controlled cooling) through the premelting and melting regime, ensuring rapid heating rates that do not allow full atomic equilibration.
drafts.conditions: Experiments should be performed on nanoparticles of comparable size (<20 nm) under identical heating protocols. A controlled comparison should be made between HEA nanoparticles and simpler bimetallic (or monometallic) nanoparticles under the same thermal conditions.
drafts.structural_mediator: The high configurational entropy, which leads to severe lattice distortion combined with inhibited atom mobility, creates uniformly distributed potential melting nucleation sites across the nanoparticle.
drafts.mechanism: Due to limited atomic mobility in the solid state, the energy input during rapid heating causes the onset of melting to occur stochastically and simultaneously at multiple sites. The high entropy drives a homogeneous, single-phase melting transition despite the different local melting tendencies of individual elements. This contrasts with conventional particles where distinct elemental melting or segregation can occur.
drafts.predicted_outcome: HEA nanoparticles will display a broader, more gradual (premelting) transition with an extended coexistence of solid and liquid-like features, and they will retain a more uniform chemical mixing upon cooling. In contrast, bimetallic or monometallic nanoparticles will show sharper phase transitions accompanied by localized segregation.
drafts.baseline: Bimetallic or single-metal nanoparticles (e.g., Ag, Au, Al, or Pd), which typically exhibit sharp phase transitions and local compositional segregation during melting.
drafts.boundary: This hypothesis applies to nanoparticles where the heating rates are high enough to limit atom mobility, and for particle sizes where surface-to-volume effects and lattice strain are significant (roughly <20 nm). It is relevant under non-equilibrium conditions where the entropic stabilization dominates over enthalpic segregation forces.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform in situ heating experiments (using high-resolution X-ray diffraction, transmission electron microscopy with elemental mapping, and differential scanning calorimetry) on both HEA nanoparticles and bimetallic nanoparticles under identical rapid heating and cooling conditions. Compare the temperature range and uniformity of the melting transition, as well as post-cooling compositional homogeneity.
measurements: Temperature-resolved XRD patterns to monitor phase transition onset and breadth
In situ TEM imaging with EDS mapping to assess uniformity of elemental distribution during melting
DSC curves to quantify the melting enthalpy and match the onset of melting
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If HEA nanoparticles exhibit a similarly sharp melting transition and/or show clear evidence of elemental phase segregation (comparable to bimetallic systems) rather than a broadened, homogeneous melting behavior, then the hypothesis will be falsified.
